title: Watermelon
problem:
One hot summer day Pete and his friend Billy decided to buy a watermelon. They chose the biggest and the ripest one, in their opinion. After that the watermelon was weighed, and the scales showed `w` kilos. They rushed home, dying of thirst, and decided to divide the berry, however they faced a hard problem.

Pete and Billy are great fans of even numbers, that's why they want to divide the watermelon in such a way that each of the two parts weighs even number of kilos, at the same time it is not obligatory that the parts are equal in size.

Print `YES`, if the boys can divide the watermelon into two parts, each of them weighing even number of kilos; and `NO` in the opposite case.

examples.explanation: Can be divided into 2 and 6 (or 4 and 4), both even.
Only possible division is 1 and 1, which are odd numbers.

approach: An even number `w` can be divided into two even positive integers if and only if `w > 2` and `w % 2 == 0`. The number 2 cannot be divided because 2 = 1 + 1 (odd parts).

complexity.time: O(1) — constant time parity and inequality check

title: Way Too Long Words
problem:
Sometimes some words like 'localization' or 'internationalization' are so long that their writing from it in one text is quite tiresome.

Let's consider a word too long, if its length is strictly more than 10 characters. All too long words should be replaced with a special abbreviation.

This abbreviation is made like this: we write the first and the last letter of a word and between them we write the number of letters between the first and the last letters.
constraints: Each word contains 1 to 100 lowercase Latin letters
approach: Check if string length `L > 10`. If true, construct abbreviation: `first_char + to_string(L - 2) + last_char`. Otherwise print the original word unmodified.

complexity.time: O(L) per word — where L is string length

title: Team
problem: One day three best friends Petya, Vasya and Tonya decided to form a team and take part in programming contests. For each problem, each friend either is sure about the solution (1) or isn't (0). The friends only solve a problem if at least two of them are sure about the solution. Find the number of problems the friends will solve.
approach: For each problem, sum the three opinions: `p + v + t`. If `sum >= 2`, increment counter `problemsSolved`.

title: Next Round
problem: A contestant who earns a score equal to or greater than the `k-th` place finisher's score will advance to the next round, as long as the contestant earns a positive score. Calculate how many participants will advance.

examples.explanation: 5th contestant has 7 points. Contestants 1 to 6 have >= 7 points.

constraints: 0 <= a[i] <= 100, scores sorted in non-increasing order
approach: Obtain score `threshold = a[k - 1]`. Count all participants `i` where `a[i] >= threshold` and `a[i] > 0`.

title: Domino Piling
problem: You are given a rectangular board of `M * N` squares. You are also given an unlimited number of standard domino pieces of `2 * 1` squares. You are allowed to rotate the pieces. Find the maximum number of dominoes which can be placed on the board.
approach: Each domino covers exactly 2 squares. The total area is `M * N`. By integer division, at most `floor((M * N) / 2)` dominoes can be packed.

title: Bit++
problem: The classic programming language Bit++ has one variable `X`, initially 0. There are two operations: `++X` or `X++` (increments X by 1) and `--X` or `X--` (decrements X by 1). Execute `n` statements and output final value of `X`.
approach: Inspect each instruction string: if it contains `+`, increment `x`; if it contains `-`, decrement `x`.

title: Beautiful Matrix
problem: You've got a `5 * 5` matrix, consisting of 24 zeroes and a single number one. In one move, you are allowed to swap two neighboring rows or columns. Find the minimum number of moves needed to place the number one at the center of the matrix `(3, 3)`.

examples.explanation: Row 2 to 3 takes 1 move, col 5 to 3 takes 2 moves. Total = 1 + 2 = 3.

approach: Find the 1-based coordinates `(r, c)` of the cell containing 1. The Manhattan distance to center `(3, 3)` is `|r - 3| + |c - 3|`.

title: Petya and Strings
problem: Compare two strings of equal length case-insensitively. Output `-1` if the first string is less than the second, `1` if greater, or `0` if equal.
constraints: Consists of uppercase and lowercase Latin letters
approach: Convert both strings to lowercase. Compare character by character. If `s1[i] < s2[i]`, return `-1`. If `s1[i] > s2[i]`, return `1`. If identical throughout, return `0`.

complexity.time: O(L) — where L is string length

title: Helpful Maths
problem: Xenia is a beginner mathematician. Her teacher gave her a summands expression like `3+2+1`. Rearrange the summands in non-decreasing order.
approach: Extract all digit characters from the string. Sort them in ascending order. Join them with '+' separators.

title: Word Capitalization
problem: Capitalization is writing a word with its first letter as a capital letter. Capitalize the given word.
approach: Capitalize the first character using standard uppercase conversion and preserve the remainder of the word unchanged.
